title: Why “the price stays the same” is so hard to beat
text: Over a day, a coin’s typical move is a few percent up or down, and the direction is close to a coin flip. A forecast that says “no change” is wrong by exactly that move. A model that adds a guess about direction is wrong by the move plus or minus its guess, and when the guess points the wrong way about half the time, it adds error instead of removing it. In our one-year backtest the model’s error at 24 and 72 hours was about 7 percent higher than doing nothing.

title: What an 80% range actually promises
text: A range labelled 80% should contain the outcome about eight times in ten, no more and no less. If it holds nine in ten it is wider than it needs to be; if it holds five in ten it pretends to know more than it does. We count how often each range held and publish the count, because a range that is never checked is decoration.

title: How far is easier than which way
text: Tomorrow’s direction is nearly unpredictable from prices alone. Tomorrow’s size of move is not: calm days tend to follow calm days, and wild days follow wild days. That is why a band built from nothing but recent volatility can score better than the uncertainty range of a large forecasting model. It knows nothing about direction, and it does not pretend to.

title: A trend filter loses less. It does not earn more
text: Holding a coin only while its recent returns are positive kept our six-year backtest out of the longest declines: the deepest loss was about half as deep. The end result was roughly the same as holding throughout. The rule’s value, if it holds up, is a calmer ride, and two long declines in six years are a small sample to prove even that.

title: Why a perfect hit rate can mean almost nothing
text: Hourly forecasts for the next 24 hours overlap: thirty of them cover little more than two days of market. If the model said “up” every time during one rally, it was right thirty times about the same single move. Count the days, not the forecasts, before trusting a hit rate.

title: A reason for every trade, including the decision to wait
text: Each hour the paper portfolios record a decision per coin with the market checks behind it. Most hours the decision is to do nothing, because trading costs are real: a forecast has to clear fees, slippage, the spread and a safety margin before it justifies a buy. Doing nothing is a position too, and it is written down like any other.

title: What a headline classification is, and is not
text: The news radar labels a headline by coin, event type and tone. That describes the text. It is not a statement that the news is true, and it is not a price forecast. In the paper portfolios a material negative headline can only block a buy; it never adds or subtracts percent from a forecast.

title: Why we publish results that went against us
text: A record that only shows the wins cannot be told apart from luck. Every forecast here is stored before its deadline, scored afterwards and left on the page, including the ones that missed badly. That is slower and less flattering than a highlight reel, and it is the only way a number on this site can mean anything.
